opus-5.5.text:
I think people in Silicon Valley roughly fall into a few camps on simulation, and it's actually one of the more interesting debates in robotics right now.

One camp, and I'd say I've been closely associated with it given my background in computer graphics and physics simulation, believes simulation is essential. The argument is simple: real robot data is extremely expensive and slow to collect. You need hardware, operators, maintenance, and robots break. In simulation you can run thousands of environments in parallel, faster than real time, and you can try dangerous or rare scenarios that you'd never want to try on a real robot. For locomotion especially, sim-to-real has been a huge success. Most of the agile legged robots you see walking, running, and recovering from pushes today were trained largely in simulation with reinforcement learning, then transferred to hardware.

The second camp is more skeptical, and they're mostly coming from manipulation. Their view is that the sim-to-real gap is too large for contact-rich tasks: deformable objects, cloth, liquids, friction, the visual complexity of real homes. Modeling all of that accurately is extremely hard, and if your simulator is wrong, the policy learns to exploit the simulator's mistakes. So they say: just collect real-world data at scale, through teleoperation or human videos, and let large models learn from that. A lot of the recent foundation-model startups lean this way.

And then there's an emerging third view, which I find the most exciting: simulation itself is being redefined. Instead of hand-built physics engines, people are exploring learned world models, generative video models that can act as simulators. The idea is that the "simulator" might eventually be a neural network trained on enormous amounts of video, so you get realism from data and scalability from computation at the same time.

My own take is that it's not either-or. Real data grounds you in reality; you can't avoid it. But real data alone won't scale to the amount robotics ultimately needs. So the question isn't whether to use simulation, but which kind of simulation, for which part of the problem, and how to mix it with real data. For locomotion the answer is already fairly clear. For dexterous manipulation, I think it's still open, and whoever figures out the right mix will have a big advantage.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts camps by their views on simulation’s value, sim-to-real limitations, and emerging simulator types. It does not identify the proportion of simulation data in the overall data mixture as the main difference.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the differences are actually pretty sharp, and they map onto people's backgrounds more than anything else.

If you come from the computer vision or language side, your instinct is that data is something you collect. You scrape the internet, you label, you scale. So when those folks move into robotics, their first reaction to simulation is skepticism. They'll say, the sim-to-real gap is real, the physics isn't accurate, the visuals look fake, why would I train on something that isn't the actual world? For them, simulation feels like a crutch you use until you can afford real data.

People who come from reinforcement learning or classical robotics, which is more my background, see it the opposite way. We spent years watching real robots break, needing a human to reset the scene every episode, getting maybe a few hundred trials a day. Simulation is the thing that lets you run millions of trials overnight, randomize everything, and actually explore. So for us the question was never whether to use simulation. It was how to close the gap.

And then there's a third group that's emerged more recently, which is the people who think in terms of generative models. For them simulation is just another kind of data generation. A physics engine, a learned world model, a video model, they're all approximations of the world with different tradeoffs. That framing has actually been healthy because it stopped the argument from being physics-sim versus real-data and turned it into a question about which approximation is cheap enough and accurate enough for a given task.

What I've noticed in practice, at Google and in the startups around the Bay, is that the most effective teams don't pick a side. They use simulation for the things it's good at, like locomotion, large-scale randomization, rare failure cases you can't safely collect. And they use real data for the things where fidelity really matters, like contact-rich manipulation and perception in cluttered homes. The debate in Silicon Valley is loud, but the actual engineering has converged on being pragmatic about it.

r001.rationale: The response describes differences by practitioners’ backgrounds and which tasks they use simulation or real data for, but it does not identify the proportion of simulation data in the overall data mixture as the main difference.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest difference is how much people expect simulation to do. Some see it mainly as a testing tool: you develop a system using real-world data, then use simulation to check whether it works in different situations. Others see simulation as a way to generate the experience the system needs to learn in the first place.

For robotics, that distinction matters. Collecting data on a physical robot takes time, and failures can damage the hardware. In simulation, you can run many experiments in parallel and let the robot fail repeatedly. But then you have to ask: does what it learns transfer to the real world?

That leads to another difference in approach. Some people emphasize making the simulator as accurate as possible. Others emphasize variation—changing friction, mass, delays, and other conditions so the policy doesn’t depend on one perfectly modeled environment. I see those approaches as complementary. The important question is not simply whether the simulation looks realistic, but whether it captures the things that matter for the task.

r001.rationale: The response frames the main difference as whether simulation is used for testing or for generating learning experience. It does not identify the proportion of simulation data in the overall data mixture as the main difference.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest difference is whether people see simulation as a way to test a system or as a way to train it. If you’re using it for testing, you care a lot about whether it faithfully reproduces the real world. If you’re using it for training, the question becomes: does the experience you generate help the system perform better in the real world?

Those goals overlap, but they aren’t identical. A very realistic simulator can still miss something important, and a simplified simulator can be useful if it captures the right things. So I wouldn’t judge simulation data just by how realistic it looks or how much of it you can generate. I’d look at what the model learns from it and then validate that on the real system.

r001.rationale: The candidate frames the main difference as using simulation for testing versus training. It does not identify the proportion of simulation data in the overall data mixture.
